$comment: The catalog of plugins cxagent knows about. One entry per plugin; the ones cxagent itself
releases also have a directory beside this file.
MACHINE-READABLE ON PURPOSE. The plugin picker reads this to show what is available and where
to get it, so it does not have to parse a README or hardcode a list. Keep it truthful by hand
until something generates it — an entry naming an asset no release carries is worse than no
entry at all. CatalogTests checks each entry against the plugin's own sidecar.
FIRST-PARTY AND THIRD-PARTY ENTRIES DIFFER IN ONE FIELD: `source`. A first-party plugin says
`{ "kind": "release", "asset": "..." }` and is fetched from cxagent's own release, pinned
to the version being installed. Anything else names where it actually lives, and the fields
below stop being a formality: nobody needs telling who wrote a plugin that ships in the same
zip as the binary, and everybody needs telling for one that does not.
WHAT THE HASH IS AND IS NOT. `sha256` is over the downloaded artifact, and proves the bytes
arrived unaltered. It says nothing about who wrote them — that is `publisher` and
`repository`, which are claims a reader judges, not facts a client can verify. The separate
hash the load prompt shows is over the INSTALLED load set, and answers a different question:
has anything changed since you approved it.
generated from the artifacts themselves. A plugin hosted elsewhere DOES carry `sha256` here,
A worked entry for each `source` shape lives in RELEASING.md, beside the steps for adding
one. This file carries only plugins that actually exist.
`checksums` stays beside it: SHA256SUMS is generated from the artifacts themselves at release
time, so it is the authority. This field is the convenience — a client that has only this file
can check a download without fetching a second asset.
PLATFORMS. A managed plugin is portable MSIL: one build runs everywhere cxagent does, so it says
`platforms: ["any"]` and has a single `source`. An ABI plugin is a native library and is NOT
portable — a .so does not load on Windows, and a publisher may ship linux-x64 and nothing else.
So an ABI entry lists the RIDs it actually has and keys its downloads by the same names:
`sources: { "linux-x64": {...}, "osx-arm64": {...} }` instead of one `source`. A client picks
the entry matching its own RID and, finding none, says the plugin is not available for this
machine — which is a better answer than downloading a library that cannot load.
RIDs are .NET's own (linux-x64, linux-arm64, osx-x64, osx-arm64, win-x64, win-arm64), the same
vocabulary the release matrix uses. `platforms` and the keys of `sources` must agree; a plugin
claiming a platform it has no download for is worse than one that does not claim it.
`sha256` IS NULL FOR THE BUILT-IN PLUGIN, deliberately and for now. A hash here would have to be
the hash of the artifact a release built, and nothing writes it back: install.sh verifies against
the release's own SHA256SUMS instead, which is fetched from the same release as the zip. That is
the weaker check — it catches a corrupted download, not a compromised release — and the stronger
one needs a value reviewed in a commit rather than fetched at install time. Left open on purpose.
A `url` source DOES carry its own sha256: it pins an exact file somewhere this project does not
control, so the hash is the only thing vouching for it, and whoever adds the entry has the file.
HOW A CLIENT DOWNLOADS ONE. A `url` source is fetched as written. A `release` source uses
`latest` — GitHub's own always-current alias, which resolves to the newest release carrying that
asset. There is deliberately no way to ask for a SPECIFIC release's copy: every release carries
the plugin (an unchanged one is re-uploaded byte for byte), and the plugin's version tracks the
plugin rather than the release, so 'the latest' is the only version anyone needs to name.

plugins.name: csharp-lsp
plugins.description: Go-to-definition, find-references and diagnostics for C#, backed by a language server. Crosses project boundaries: a reference in a test project resolves into the project under test.

requires.description: A C# language server on PATH. csharp-ls is the default and needs no configuration.

settings.server: The language server command. Defaults to csharp-ls.
settings.args: Arguments for it. OmniSharp needs ["-lsp"]; csharp-ls needs none, or ["--features","razor-support"] to analyse .razor and .cshtml.
